title: Lecture 4 - 3: Evaluating Models with Plots
text:
Evaluating models with plots

Numeric metrics tell us how well a model performs.
Plots help us understand how the model is behaving.
Visualizations can help us:

Examine model fit.
Identify patterns in errors.
Compare models.
Detect possible overfitting or underfitting.
Understand how features affect predictions.




Classification

Decision boundary plot
ROC curve
Confusion matrix


Regression

Prediction error plot
Partial dependence plot

title: Lecture 4 - 3: Evaluating Models with Plots
text:
Decision boundary plots

A decision boundary separates regions of the feature space associated with different classes.
A decision boundary plot shows how a classifier assigns observations to different classes.
Particularly useful when there are two or three input features.
We can use the plot to assess:

Whether the boundary makes sense.
Whether the model is too simple.
Whether the model may be overfitting.

title: Lecture 4 - 3: Evaluating Models with Plots
text:
Comparing decision boundaries


Logistic Regression

Produces a relatively simple, linear boundary.
Easier to interpret.
May underfit when the relationship between features and classes is complex.


k-Nearest Neighbors

Can produce more irregular boundaries.
Flexible enough to capture local patterns.
Very irregular boundaries may indicate overfitting.


Question: Which model would you trust more if the decision boundary closely follows every training observation?

title: Lecture 4 - 3: Evaluating Models with Plots
text:
Interpreting a decision boundary

Each region of the plot corresponds to a predicted class.
The boundary indicates where the model changes its prediction.
The observed data points allow us to compare:

Predicted class
Actual class

Misclassified observations appear in a region belonging to the wrong class.

Question: If an observation lies in the “Diabetic” region but is actually nondiabetic, what has happened?

The model has made a false positive.

title: Lecture 4 - 3: Evaluating Models with Plots
text:
ROC curves and AUC

An ROC curve evaluates a binary classifier across many classification thresholds.
The x-axis shows the False Positive Rate (FPR):

\[
FPR = \frac{FP}{FP + TN}
\]

The y-axis shows the True Positive Rate (TPR), also called recall:

\[
TPR = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}
\]

Each point on the ROC curve corresponds to a different decision threshold.

title: Lecture 4 - 3: Evaluating Models with Plots
text:
Understanding the ROC curve


Perfect classifier

AUC = 1.0
TPR = 1
FPR = 0
Curve reaches the upper-left corner.

Random classifier

AUC = 0.5
ROC curve follows the diagonal.
No useful ability to distinguish the classes.


Good classifier

ROC curve lies above the diagonal.
Higher AUC generally indicates better ranking performance.
Example:

\[
AUC = 0.84
\]

Important: AUC summarizes performance across thresholds; it does not select the optimal threshold for you.

title: Lecture 4 - 3: Evaluating Models with Plots
section: What happens when we change the threshold?
text:
What happens when we change the threshold?

Classification models often produce a score or probability.
We convert that score into a class using a threshold.
Higher threshold:

Fewer positive predictions.
Usually fewer false positives.
Usually more false negatives.

Lower threshold:

More positive predictions.
Usually more true positives.
Usually more false positives.




High threshold

Higher precision
Lower recall
Useful when false positives are costly


Low threshold

Higher recall
Lower precision
Useful when false negatives are costly

title: Lecture 4 - 3: Evaluating Models with Plots
text:
ROC curve: an important distinction

AUC evaluates how well the model ranks positive observations above negative observations.
The ROC curve shows the trade-off between TPR and FPR across thresholds.
AUC can tell us which model has better overall discrimination.
AUC does not tell us which threshold to use in practice.

Question: Suppose missing a positive case is extremely costly. Would we necessarily choose the threshold that gives the highest AUC?
No. AUC evaluates the model across thresholds; the operational threshold should reflect the cost of false positives vs. false negatives.

title: Lecture 4 - 3: Evaluating Models with Plots
text:
ROC curves in scikit-learn
from sklearn.metrics import RocCurveDisplay

RocCurveDisplay.from_estimator(
    model,
    X_test,
    y_test
)

from_estimator() uses the fitted model to generate predictions.
The ROC curve is created using the model’s prediction scores.
We can also calculate the AUC directly:

from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

y_score = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]

auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, y_score)

print("AUC:", auc)

title: Lecture 4 - 3: Evaluating Models with Plots
text:
Prediction error plots

A prediction error plot, also called a residual plot, shows:

Predicted values on the x-axis.
Prediction errors (residuals) on the y-axis.


\[
e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i
\]

A reference line at:

\[
e_i = 0
\]
is usually included.

We use the plot to examine whether the model’s errors show a systematic pattern.

title: Lecture 4 - 3: Evaluating Models with Plots
section: What does a good prediction error plot look like?
text:
What does a good prediction error plot look like?
Ideal pattern

Residuals are randomly scattered around zero.
Points appear both above and below zero.
No obvious relationship between predicted values and residuals.
Similar spread across the range of predictions.

Warning signs

Curved pattern → possible nonlinear relationship.
Funnel-shaped pattern → changing error variance.
Large isolated residuals → possible outliers.
Systematic pattern → model may be missing important information.

title: Lecture 4 - 3: Evaluating Models with Plots
text:
Interpreting prediction error plots


Random pattern

Residuals centered around zero.
No obvious structure.
Model may be adequately capturing the relationship.


Systematic pattern

Residuals follow a curve or other pattern.
Suggests the model may be missing something.
Consider:

Nonlinear features.
Additional predictors.
A different model.



Question: What might a funnel-shaped residual plot tell us?

The variability of the prediction errors changes across the range of predicted values.

title: Lecture 4 - 3: Evaluating Models with Plots
text:
Creating a prediction error plot
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

model = LinearRegression()
model.fit(X, y)

y_pred = model.predict(X)

residuals = y - y_pred

plt.scatter(y_pred, residuals)
plt.axhline(0, color="black", linestyle="--")

plt.xlabel("Predicted values")
plt.ylabel("Residuals")
plt.show()

y_pred contains the model’s predictions.
residuals measures how far each prediction is from the observed value.
We look for patterns, not just the average size of the errors.

title: Lecture 4 - 3: Evaluating Models with Plots
text:
Partial dependence plots

A partial dependence plot (PDP) shows how an input feature affects the model’s average prediction.
We vary one feature while keeping the other features at their observed values.
The model makes predictions for these modified observations.
We then average the predictions.

For feature \(x_j\):
\[
PD(x_j)
=
\frac{1}{n}
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
f(x_j, x_{i,-j})
\]

\(x_j\) = feature being investigated.
\(x_{i,-j}\) = the other features for observation \(i\).

title: Lecture 4 - 3: Evaluating Models with Plots
text:
Interpreting a partial dependence plot

A PDP answers:


“On average, how does changing this feature affect the model’s prediction?”



Positive relationship

PDP increases as the feature increases.
Higher feature values are associated with higher predictions.


Negative relationship

PDP decreases as the feature increases.
Higher feature values are associated with lower predictions.



A nonlinear curve indicates that the model’s relationship with the feature changes across its range.
PDPs describe the model’s behavior, not necessarily a causal relationship.

title: Lecture 4 - 3: Evaluating Models with Plots
section: Partial dependence and the observed data
text:
Partial dependence and the observed data

PDPs are most reliable where we have many observations.
Predictions at values far outside the observed data can be misleading.
It is useful to show the distribution of the feature along the x-axis.

Deciles

Divide the observed distribution into ten approximately equal groups.
Vertical marks can show where observations occur.

Question: Why should we be cautious about interpreting a PDP where there are very few observations?

title: Lecture 4 - 3: Evaluating Models with Plots
text:
Partial dependence in scikit-learn
from sklearn.inspection import PartialDependenceDisplay

PartialDependenceDisplay.from_estimator(
    model,
    X,
    features=[0]
)

plt.show()

model must already be fitted.
X contains the input features.
features=[0] requests the PDP for the first feature.
We can request multiple features:

PartialDependenceDisplay.from_estimator(
    model,
    X,
    features=[0, 1, 2]
)

title: Lecture 4 - 2: Regression Metrics
text:
What is a loss function?

A loss function measures how close a model’s predictions are to the actual values.
Regression models are fitted by selecting weights that minimize the loss.
Common regression loss functions:

Absolute loss (L1)
Squared loss (L2)
Huber loss
Quantile loss

The choice of loss function affects how the model responds to large errors and outliers.

title: Lecture 4 - 2: Regression Metrics
text:
Residuals and loss

The residual (prediction error) is the difference between the observed and predicted values: \[e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i\]
A loss function transforms the residual into a measure of error.
Small loss → prediction is close to the observed value.
Large loss → prediction is far from the observed value.
During model fitting, we choose parameters that minimize the overall loss.

title: Lecture 4 - 2: Regression Metrics
text:
Absolute loss

Absolute loss measures the absolute value of the prediction error: \[L_1(y, \hat{y}) = |y - \hat{y}|\]
Also called L1 loss.
All errors are penalized proportionally to their size.
The Mean Absolute Error (MAE) is the average absolute loss: \[MAE = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|y_i-\hat{y}_i|\]
Less sensitive to outliers than squared loss.

title: Lecture 4 - 2: Regression Metrics
text:
Squared loss

Squared loss squares the prediction error: \[L_2(y, \hat{y}) = (y-\hat{y})^2\]
Also called L2 loss.
Large errors receive much larger penalties.
The Mean Squared Error (MSE) is the average squared loss: \[MSE = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2\]
Ordinary linear regression is typically fitted using least squares, which minimizes squared loss.

title: Lecture 4 - 2: Regression Metrics
section: Why does squared loss care about outliers?
text:
Why does squared loss care about outliers?

Squaring an error makes large prediction errors disproportionately important.
Example:

Error of 2 → squared loss = 4
Error of 10 → squared loss = 100

A single extreme observation can therefore have a large influence on the fitted regression line.
Question: Which loss would you prefer when your data contain substantial outliers?

title: Lecture 4 - 2: Regression Metrics
text:
Huber loss

Huber loss combines squared and absolute loss.
For small errors, it behaves like squared loss.
For large errors, it behaves like absolute loss.
This gives us:

Smooth optimization near zero.
Less sensitivity to outliers than squared loss.

A hyperparameter \(\delta\) controls where the loss transitions from quadratic to linear.

title: Lecture 4 - 2: Regression Metrics
section: Huber loss: the best of both?
text:
Huber loss: the best of both?
\[
L_\delta(e) =
\begin{cases}
\frac{1}{2}e^2, & |e| \leq \delta \\
\delta\left(|e|-\frac{1}{2}\delta\right), & |e| > \delta
\end{cases}
\]

Small errors: quadratic → similar to squared loss.
Large errors: linear → similar to absolute loss.
Smaller \(\delta\): Huber behaves more like absolute loss.
Larger \(\delta\): Huber behaves more like squared loss.

title: Lecture 4 - 2: Regression Metrics
text:
Quantile loss

Quantile loss allows us to penalize underprediction and overprediction differently.
Useful for quantile regression, where we predict a specific quantile of the target distribution.
The loss depends on the quantile \(\tau\) and whether the prediction is above or below the observed value.
Examples:

\(\tau=0.50\) → median regression.
\(\tau=0.75\) → 75th percentile.
\(\tau=0.90\) → 90th percentile.

title: Lecture 4 - 2: Regression Metrics
text:
Quantile loss and asymmetric penalties

For small quantiles, overpredictions receive a larger penalty.
For large quantiles, underpredictions receive a larger penalty.
At \(\tau=0.50\), underprediction and overprediction are penalized equally.
Question: If we are predicting the 90th percentile, should an underprediction or an overprediction receive the larger penalty?

title: Lecture 4 - 2: Regression Metrics
section: Fitting a model with Huber loss
text:
Fitting a model with Huber loss
from sklearn.linear_model import HuberRegressor

model_huber = HuberRegressor()
model_huber.fit(X, y)

y_pred = model_huber.predict(X)

HuberRegressor() fits a linear model using Huber loss.
Small prediction errors are treated similarly to squared loss.
Large prediction errors are treated more like absolute loss.
This makes the model less sensitive to outliers.

model_lr = LinearRegression()
model_huber = HuberRegressor()

model_lr.fit(X, y)
model_huber.fit(X, y)

y_pred_lr = model_lr.predict(X)
y_pred_huber = model_huber.predict(X)

print("Linear Regression MSE:",
      mean_squared_error(y, y_pred_lr))

print("Huber Regression MSE:",
      mean_squared_error(y, y_pred_huber))

A loss function tells us how costly a prediction error is.
Absolute loss is more robust to outliers.

title: Lecture 4 - 2: Regression Metrics
text:
Rationale

MAPE: Measures error relative to the actual value, so a $30K error on a $60K house counts much more than the same error on a $500K house.
MAE: Gives the average absolute error in the same units as the target—here, exam points.
MSE/RMSE: Squares errors, giving disproportionately more weight to large errors. MSE penalizes them most directly; RMSE is easier to interpret because it is in the original units.
R² (R-squared): Measures the proportion of variation in the target explained by the model, making it useful for comparing how much variation in claim amounts the models account for.

text:

For interpretability: prefer RMSE or MAPE
When you want to discourage large error: MSE is common
For fair comparison: r2 provides a normalized score similar to accuracy in classification.

For imbalanced scales: MAPE helps when proportional error matters more than absolute error.

title: Lecture 5: Model Validation
section: How Do We Know If a Model Works?
text:
How Do We Know If a Model Works?
We split the data into separate sets so that we can answer three different questions:

Train — Can the model learn?
Use the training data to estimate the model’s parameters.
Validate — Which model should we use?
Use the validation data to compare models, select among alternatives, and tune hyperparameters.
Test — How well does the final model generalize?
Use unseen test data to obtain an unbiased estimate of the final model’s performance.

Train → Choose → Evaluate

title: Lecture 5: Model Validation
text:
Why is Cross-Validation Important?

Preventing Overfitting: A model that memorizes training data will fail on new, unseen data.
Realistic Performance Estimation: Evaluating on training data gives overly optimistic accuracy.
Data Efficiency: Single train/test splits can lead to high variance depending on which samples fall into which set.
Robustness: Cross-validation tests performance across multiple subsets to ensure reliability.

Fraction (Typical)

title: Lecture 5: Model Validation
text:
Stratified Splits
A sampling method that ensures each fold or split contains approximately the same percentage of samples of each target class as the complete dataset.
When to Use?

Imbalanced Datasets: e.g., Fraud detection (99% normal, 1% fraud).
Small Datasets: Random splits might omit rare classes entirely from train or validation sets.
Classification Tasks: Standard practice for single-label and multi-label classification.

title: Lecture 5: Model Validation
section: Code: Creating Train, Validation, and Test Sets
text:
Code: Creating Train, Validation, and Test Sets
In scikit-learn, we can perform a 3-way split by calling train_test_split twice:

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris

# Load dataset
X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)

# Step 1: Split into Train+Val (80%) and Test (20%)
X_train_val, X_test, y_train_val, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.20, random_state=42, stratify=y
)

# Step 2: Split Train+Val into Train (75% of 80% = 60%) and Validation (25% of 80% = 20%)
X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val = train_test_split(
    X_train_val, y_train_val, test_size=0.25, random_state=42, stratify=y_train_val
)

print(f"Train: {X_train.shape[0]} | Val: {X_val.shape[0]} | Test: {X_test.shape[0]}")

title: Lecture 5: Model Validation
text:
K-Fold Cross-Validation
Split the training dataset into \(K\) equal-sized subsets (folds).

Train the model on \(K-1\) folds.
Validate the model on the remaining \(1\) fold.
Repeat \(K\) times, using each fold as validation once.
Compute the final performance metric as the average across all \(K\) trials:

\[\text{CV Score} = \frac{1}{K} \sum_{i=1}^{K} \text{Score}_i\]

Common Values for \(K\): \(K=5\) or \(K=10\) (good trade-off between computational cost and bias/variance).

title: Lecture 5: Model Validation
text:
Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOO-CV)
An extreme case of \(K\)-Fold CV where \(K = N\) (\(N\) = total number of samples).

For each iteration:
Train on \(N-1\) samples.
Test on the single \(1\) remaining sample.
Advantages:
Unbiased performance estimation (uses almost all data for training).
Fully deterministic (no randomness in splitting).
Disadvantages:
High computational cost (fits \(N\) separate models).
High variance in evaluation error.

title: Lecture 5: Model Validation
text:
Code: Leave-One-Out CV in Scikit-Learn
from sklearn.model_selection import LeaveOneOut, cross_val_score
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris

# Load dataset
X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)

# Initialize LeaveOneOut iterator
loo = LeaveOneOut()
model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)

# Evaluate using LOO (fits 150 times for Iris dataset)
scores = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=loo, scoring='accuracy')

print(f"Number of fits (N): {len(scores)}")
print(f"LOO-CV Mean Accuracy: {scores.mean():.4f}")

title: Lecture 5: Model Validation
text:
Code: Implementing Cross-Validation in Scikit-Learn
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, KFold, StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

model = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42)

# Standard 5-Fold CV
scores = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=5, scoring='accuracy')
print(f"5-Fold CV Accuracy: {scores.mean():.4f} (+/- {scores.std():.4f})")

# Custom Stratified K-Fold
skf = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
skf_scores = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=skf, scoring='accuracy')
print(f"Stratified 5-Fold Accuracy: {skf_scores.mean():.4f}")

title: Lecture 5: Model Validation
text:
Model Selection
Model Selection is the process of selecting the optimal machine learning algorithm (or architecture) among a set of candidate models for a given problem.
Examples of candidate models:

Logistic Regression vs. Support Vector Machines vs. Decision Trees vs. Random Forests.

Goal
Identify the model architecture that generalizes best to unseen data.

title: Lecture 5: Model Validation
text:
What Makes a Good Model?
When comparing candidate models, consider:

Strong performance — high accuracy, low mean squared error, etc.
Consistent performance — similar results across cross-validation or different data splits.
Reasonable assumptions — model assumptions are appropriate and not seriously violated.
Interpretability — the model is understandable when interpretation is important.

Key Idea
There is often no single best model.
We want a model that generalizes well while balancing:
Performance + Consistency + Reasonable assumptions

title: Lecture 5: Model Validation
text:
Bias–Variance Tradeoff
A model’s ability to generalize depends on two sources of error:

Bias — error from a model that is too simple to capture important patterns.
Variance — error from a model that is too sensitive to the particular training data.

The Tradeoff

High bias → model underfits the data.
High variance → model overfits the data.
Low bias + low variance → better potential to generalize to unseen data.

The goal is not to minimize training error alone.

But to Choose a model that captures meaningful patterns without fitting noise.

title: Lecture 5: Model Validation
section: Impact of Splits on Performance & Parameter Estimates
text:
Impact of Splits on Performance & Parameter Estimates
Single train/test splits can lead to volatile conclusions:

Metric Instability: A lucky or unlucky split can inflate or deflate accuracy by several percentage points.
Parameter Sensitivity: Model coefficients (or tree structures) vary wildly depending on which samples end up in the training set.
Cross-Validation Solution: Averaging metrics across \(K\) folds reduces estimate variance and provides a confidence interval (\(\text{mean} \pm \text{std}\)).

title: Lecture 5: Model Validation
section: Steps for Model Selection with Cross-Validation
text:
Steps for Model Selection with Cross-Validation

Split Data: Reserve a holdout Test Set (\(10\% - 20\%\)).
Define Candidate Models: List algorithm families to compare.
Evaluate via CV: Perform \(K\)-Fold CV on the training set for each candidate.
Compare Performance: Compute mean and standard deviation of validation metrics across folds.
Select Best Model: Choose the model family with the superior CV score.
Refit & Test: Re-train selected model on the entire training set and evaluate on the holdout Test Set.

title: Lecture 5: Model Validation
section: Code: Implementing Model Selection with CV
text:
Code: Implementing Model Selection with CV
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

models = {
    "Logistic Regression": LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000),
    "Support Vector Machine": SVC(),
    "Random Forest": RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42)
}

# Evaluate candidates on training portion
for name, clf in models.items():
    cv_scores = cross_val_score(clf, X_train_val, y_train_val, cv=5)
    print(f"{name}: Mean CV Accuracy = {cv_scores.mean():.4f} (std: {cv_scores.std():.4f})")

title: Lecture 5: Model Validation
text:
Hyperparameter vs. Parameter & Model Tuning
Parameters vs. Hyperparameters

Parameters: Learned directly from data during training (e.g., weights \(w\), bias \(b\), split points in trees).
Hyperparameters: Configured before training to control learning behavior (e.g., learning rate \(\alpha\), \(C\) in SVM, max_depth in Decision Trees).

Model Tuning
The process of searching for the combination of hyperparameters that yields optimal model validation performance.

title: Lecture 5: Model Validation
text:
sklearn methods

sklearn provides two main methods for hyperparameter optimization
Grid Search — systematically evaluates every combination in a predefined grid.
Random Search — randomly samples configurations from specified distributions.

The choice of search strategy depends largely on the size and structure of the hyperparameter space.

title: Lecture 5: Model Validation
section: Setting a Tuning Grid & Grid Search
text:
Setting a Tuning Grid & Grid Search
A Tuning Grid defines a discrete search space over hyperparameter values.
param_grid = {
    'n_estimators': [50, 100, 200],
    'max_depth': [3, 5, 10, None],
    'min_samples_split': [2, 5]
}

GridSearchCV: Evaluates all \(3 \times 4 \times 2 = 24\) combinations using \(K\)-Fold cross-validation.
Selection: Picks the combination that yields the highest mean CV score.

from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

# Define candidate model and search space

title: Lecture 5: Model Validation
text:
Interpreting Validation Curves
A Validation Curve plots training and validation scores against a single hyperparameter’s values.
Validation curves are useful for detecting overfitting: - Hyperparameters that are overfitted will have high training scores and low validation scores. - Optimal hyperparameters will perform well on the training sets and the validation sets.

Code: Plotting a Validation Curve

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.model_selection import validation_curve
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

param_range = np.arange(1, 11)
train_scores, val_scores = validation_curve(
    DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42), X_train_val, y_train_val,
    param_name="max_depth", param_range=param_range, cv=5, scoring="accuracy"
)

train_mean, val_mean = np.mean(train_scores, axis=1), np.mean(val_scores, axis=1)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
plt.plot(param_range, train_mean, label="Training Score", color="blue", marker="o")
plt.plot(param_range, val_mean, label="Validation Score", color="red", marker="o")
plt.xlabel("Max Depth")
plt.ylabel("Accuracy")
plt.title("Validation Curve for Decision Tree")
plt.legend(loc="best")
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()

title: Lecture 6: Model Improvement
text:
Preparing Data for Machine Learning

Data quality is a measure of how well data is used to meet a specific need.
Poor data quality leads to misleading results and inaccurate predictions.
Data pre-processing changes or transforms raw data that contains missing values, noise, and other inconsistencies into a format that improves the performance of different machine learning models.

title: Lecture 6: Model Improvement
text:
Why Data Must Be Pre-processed

Algorithm Mechanics: Distance-based algorithms (k-NN, SVM, K-Means) and gradient-based methods are sensitive to feature scales and magnitudes.
Garbage In, Garbage Out: Raw real-world data is dirty, incomplete, unformatted, and noisy.
Model Efficiency & Accuracy: Proper preprocessing improves convergence speed, numerical stability, and generalizability.
Requirements of ML Frameworks: Most algorithms cannot natively handle text labels or missing values (NaN).

title: Lecture 6: Model Improvement
section: The Six Dimensions of Data Quality
text:
The Six Dimensions of Data Quality

Accuracy: Is the data correct and reflective of reality?
Completeness: Are there missing records, missing fields, or incomplete attributes?
Consistency: Does the data conflict across different systems or tables?
Timeliness: Is the information up-to-date for the current problem?
Validity: Does the data follow defined business rules, types, and ranges?
Uniqueness: Are there duplicated records or overlapping entities?

title: Lecture 6: Model Improvement
text:
Data Preprocessing Tasks
Data preprocessing is important in machine learning because data quality directly affects model performance and predictions.






Note


Many classification algorithms are distance-based, meaning that their results can be affected by the units and scales of the input features.
### Common Preprocessing Tasks

Data Cleaning: Addresses missing values, duplicate observations, and incorrectly formatted data.
Data Integration: Combines data from multiple sources into a unified dataset.
Data Reduction: Reduces the dimensionality or size of a dataset while retaining important information.
Data Transformation: Converts features into a format or scale suitable for a particular model or algorithm.

title: Lecture 6: Model Improvement
text:
Types of Missing Data Mechanisms
Understanding why data is missing dictates how to fix it.

MCAR (Missing Completely at Random):
Missingness is independent of both observed and unobserved data.
Example: A sensor battery dies randomly.
MAR (Missing at Random):
Missingness depends systematically on observed data, but not the missing value itself.
Example: Men are less likely to report depression scores, but within men, missingness is random.
MNAR (Missing Not at Random):
Missingness depends directly on the unobserved value itself.
Example: High earners refuse to reveal their high income on surveys.

title: Lecture 6: Model Improvement
text:
Deletion Strategies: Listwise vs. Pairwise
When dealing with missing values, simple deletion might be considered:
Listwise Deletion (Complete Case Analysis)

Drops the entire row/record if any attribute contains a missing value.
Pros: Simple, unbiased under MCAR.
Cons: Severe loss of sample size and potential bias under MAR/MNAR.

Pairwise Deletion

Keeps the row, dropping missing values only when analyzing specific pairs of variables (e.g., during correlation calculation).
Pros: Preserves more data points.
Cons: Leads to inconsistent sample sizes (\(N\)) across different calculations; covariance matrices can become non-positive definite.

title: Lecture 6: Model Improvement
text:
The ML Workflow & Feature Removal
Where Feature Transformation Fits
\[\text{Raw Data} \longrightarrow \text{Cleaning} \longrightarrow \mathbf{\text{Feature Transformation / Scaling}} \longrightarrow \text{Feature Selection} \longrightarrow \text{Model Training}\]
When is Feature Removal Necessary?

Zero / Near-Zero Variance: A feature has the same value for almost all rows.
Extreme Multicollinearity: Two or more features are perfectly or highly correlated.
Irrelevant Features: Features with zero signal/predictive relationship with the target.
High Missingness: Features with \(\ge 50-70\%\) missing values where imputation introduces too much noise.

title: Lecture 6: Model Improvement
text:
Standardization vs. Normalization
Standardization (\(Z\)-Score Normalization)
Rescales data to centered mean (\(\mu=0\)) and unit variance (\(\sigma=1\)).
\[x' = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\]

Best when features follow a Gaussian distribution or when using algorithms that assume zero-mean features (e.g., Ridge/Lasso, PCA).

Normalization (Min-Max Scaling)
Rescales data into a fixed range, typically \([0, 1]\).
\[x' = \frac{x - x_{\min}}{x_{\max} - x_{\min}}\]

Best when features have bounded ranges, non-Gaussian distributions, or sparse data. Sensitive to extreme outliers!

title: Lecture 6: Model Improvement
text:
Categorical Encoding Strategies









Encoding
How it Works
Pros
Cons




Label / Ordinal
Maps each category to an integer (\(1, 2, 3...\))
Compact (\(1\) column)
Implies artificial ordering if data is nominal


One-Hot
Creates \(K\) binary indicator columns
No artificial order imposed
Causes high dimensionality (\(d \to \infty\)) for high-cardinality features


Binary
Converts integers to binary strings, then splits into binary columns
Compact representation (\(O(\log_2 K)\) columns)
Reduces interpretability compared to One-Hot

title: Lecture 6: Model Improvement
text:
Nonlinear Transformations & Binning
Nonlinear Transformations

Log / Box-Cox / Yeo-Johnson: Converts skewed distributions into normal distributions, stabilizing variance.
Polynomial Features: Captures non-linear interactions between variables (\(x_1^2, x_1 x_2\)).

Binning / Discretization
Converts continuous variables into categorical intervals:

Equal-Width Binning: Divides the feature range into \(k\) intervals of equal size (\(\Delta = \frac{x_{\max} - x_{\min}}{k}\)). Sensitive to outliers.
Equal-Frequency Binning: Divides data into \(k\) intervals where each bin contains approximately the same number of samples (Quantiles).

title: Lecture 6: Model Improvement
text:
Univariate vs. Multivariate Imputation

Univariate Imputation:
Predicts missing values using summary statistics calculated only from that single feature.
Methods: Mean, Median, Mode substitution.
Pros: Fast, scalable, simple.
Cons: Ignores correlations with other attributes; underestimates variance.

title: Lecture 6: Model Improvement
text:
Multivariate Imputation

Uses the entire set of observed features to estimate missing values.
Methods: k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN), MICE (IterativeImputer).
Pros: Preserves inter-feature relationships and dataset structure.
Cons: Computationally expensive; complex.

title: Lecture 6: Model Improvement
text:
Imputation Techniques Deep Dive
Mean / Median / Mode Imputation (Univariate)

Replaces NaNs in feature \(j\) with \(\text{mean}(X_j)\), \(\text{median}(X_j)\), or \(\text{mode}(X_j)\).

k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) Imputation

Finds the \(k\) most similar rows (based on Euclidean distance across non-missing attributes).
Fills missing values with the weighted or unweighted average of those \(k\) neighbors.

Multivariate Imputation by Chained Equations (MICE)

Fills missing values with initial placeholder estimates (e.g., mean).
Sets feature \(X_j\) back to NaN.
Trains a regression model predicting \(X_j\) using all other features.
Predicts missing \(X_j\). Repeats iteratively across all features until convergence.

SciKit-Learn Transformers vs Estimators
Transformers

Used for preprocessing and feature engineering.
Implement fit() and transform().
fit(X): Computes statistical parameters (e.g., \(\mu, \sigma\), categories).
transform(X): Applies parameters to transform \(X\).
Examples: StandardScaler, SimpleImputer, OneHotEncoder.

title: Lecture 6: Model Improvement
section: The Golden Rule of Feature Transformations
text:
The Golden Rule of Feature Transformations

NEVER transform the entire dataset at once!


Performing transformations across the full dataset causes Data Leakage.
Data leakage occurs when info from the validation/test set is inadvertently used to train the transformer (e.g., scaling using test set mean).
Rule:


Split data into Train and Test.
fit_transform() transformers only on Train.
transform() Test using the fitted parameters.


# CORRECT APPROACH

from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(X_test)

title: Lecture 6: Model Improvement
text:
SciKit-Learn Pipelines

Encapsulates preprocessing steps and estimators into a single execution unit.
Prevents data leakage during cross-validation.
Makes code clean, reproducible, and easily deployable.

from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier

# Define Pipeline

pipeline = make_pipeline(
SimpleImputer(strategy='median'),
StandardScaler(),
KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5)
)

# Train and Evaluate seamlessly

pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train)
accuracy = pipeline.score(X_test, y_test)

Multivariate imputation (k-NN, MICE) maintains dataset correlation structures better than univariate statistics.
Use Pipeline objects to enforce the Golden Rule and stop data leakage!

title: Lecture 4 - 1: Classification Metrics
text:
Where do loss functions fit?
Recall our supervised learning workflow:
Data → Model → Predictions → Loss → Optimization
A loss function tells us:

How bad are the model’s predictions?

During model fitting, we choose model parameters that minimize the loss.

title: Lecture 4 - 1: Classification Metrics
text:
What is a loss function?
A loss function quantifies the difference between:

what actually happened, and
what the model predicted.

In general:
\[
\text{Loss} =
\text{difference between predictions and observations}
\]
Lower loss = better predictions.

title: Lecture 4 - 1: Classification Metrics
section: Why do we need loss functions?
text:
Why do we need loss functions?
Suppose two classifiers both get 90% of observations correct.
Are they equally good?
Not necessarily.
A model might:

make confident correct predictions,
make uncertain correct predictions,
make confident incorrect predictions.

A good loss function should capture more than simply:

“Was the final class correct?”

Predicted probability

title: Lecture 4 - 1: Classification Metrics
text:
Accuracy vs. probability
Accuracy only looks at the final class:
\[
\hat y =
\begin{cases}
1 & \hat p \geq 0.5\\
0 & \hat p < 0.5
\end{cases}
\]
So these predictions all produce the same class:
\[
0.51,\quad 0.70,\quad 0.99
\]
But a loss function can distinguish between them.

For binary classification:

\(y\) = observed class, either 0 or 1
\(\hat p\) = predicted probability of class 1

Absolute loss is:
\[
L_{\text{abs}}(y,\hat p)
=
|y-\hat p|
\]
The loss is simply the distance between:

the observed class, and
the predicted probability.

Why do we need another loss?
Absolute loss treats the difference between predictions linearly.
But sometimes we want to penalize confidently wrong predictions much more strongly.

Log loss
For binary classification:
\[
L_{\text{log}}
=
-\left[
y\log(\hat p)
+
(1-y)\log(1-\hat p)
\right]
\]
This is also called:

log loss
binary cross-entropy

\[
y=1

text:
Log loss strongly penalizes confidence
For an observed class of 1:
\[
\hat p \rightarrow 1
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
L_{\text{log}}\rightarrow 0
\]
But:
\[
\hat p \rightarrow 0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
L_{\text{log}}\rightarrow \infty
\]
So log loss strongly penalizes:

being confidently wrong.

text:
Comparing absolute loss and log loss
Suppose:
\[
y=1,\quad \hat p=0.01
\]
Absolute loss:
\[

\]
Log loss:
\[
-\log(0.01)\approx4.605
\]
The log loss gives a much stronger penalty.

title: Lecture 4 - 1: Classification Metrics
text:
Why use log loss?
Log loss rewards models that:

assign high probability to the correct class,
avoid assigning tiny probability to the correct class,
produce useful probability estimates.

This makes it especially useful for models such as:

Logistic Regression
probabilistic classifiers

title: Lecture 4 - 1: Classification Metrics
text:
Log loss and logistic regression
Recall logistic regression:
\[
\hat p = P(Y=1\mid X)
\]
The model learns coefficients that produce probabilities.
The coefficients can be fitted by minimizing log loss.
So:

Logistic regression + log loss

is a natural pairing.

title: Lecture 4 - 1: Classification Metrics
text:
Precision and recall
Let’s revisit our fraud detection scenario. The circle below represents all transactions predicted as fraud by an imaginary toy model designed to detect fraudulent activity.

title: Lecture 4 - 1: Classification Metrics
text:
Intuition behind the two metrics

Precision: Of all the transactions predicted as fraud, how many were actually fraud?

High precision \(\rightarrow\) few false alarms (low false positives).

Recall: Of all the actual fraud cases, how many did the model catch?

High recall \(\rightarrow\) few missed frauds (low false negatives).

title: Lecture 4 - 1: Classification Metrics
text:
Trade-off between precision and recall

Increasing recall often decreases precision, and vice versa.

Example:

Predict “fraud” for every transaction \(\rightarrow\) perfect recall, terrible precision.

Predict “fraud” only when 100% sure \(\rightarrow\) high precision, low recall.


The right balance depends on the application and cost of errors.

title: Lecture 4 - 1: Classification Metrics
text:
F1-score

Sometimes, we want a single metric that balances precision and recall.

The F1-score is the harmonic mean of the two:

\[
F1 = 2 \times \frac{\text{Precision} \times \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}}
\]

High F1 means both precision and recall are strong.

Useful when we care about both false positives and false negatives.

What happens to precision and recall if we change the probability threshold?
Play with classification thresholds




Decreasing the threshold:

Increases the number of positive predictions
Identify more examples as “fraud” examples
More false positives, more true positives.
Recall would either stay the same or go up and precision is likely to go down (precision may increase if all the new examples after decreasing the threshold are TPs).

Increasing the threshold:

Decreases the number of positive predictions
Recall would go down or stay the same but precision is likely to go up (precision may go down if TP decrease but FP do not decrease).

Key question: How do we decide on the best threshold? It depends on the problem and trade-offs between false positives and false negatives.

PR curve

Calculate precision and recall (TPR) at every possible threshold and graph them.
Top left \(\rightarrow\) Very high threshold (strict model = high precision)
Bottom right \(\rightarrow\) Very low threshold (linient model = high recall)












We can look at all possible thresholds and plot the corresponding precision and recall!
As we lower the threshold, the classifier predicts more positives:

Recall increases because we capture more true positives.
Precision usually decreases because some of the additional positives are false positives.

As we raise the threshold, the classifier predicts fewer positives:

Precision increases because only the most confident predictions are positive.
Recall decreases because we miss more true positives.

The curve shows the trade-offs between precision and recall across all thresholds.
Ideal performance: top-right corner (high precision and high recall).
Use cases like fraud detection often require focusing on areas of the curve that favor one metric over the other (e.g., high recall for safety-critical tasks).

Average Precision (AP) Score



AP score summarizes the PR curve by calculating the area under the curve
It measures the ranking ability of a model; how well it assigns higher probabilities to positive examples than to negative ones, regardless of the specific threshold.

AUC

The area under the ROC curve (AUC) represents the probability that the model, if given a randomly chosen positive and negative example, will rank the positive higher than the negative.
